JMPR: Fenpyroximate
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Fenpyroximate
Peer review: Fenpyroximate (fruit crops, pulses and oilseeds, only)
efsa_comments:
Plant: Residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment in plant commodities are comparable. Additional metabolism studies with fenpyroximate following foliar application to citrus, apples, grapes, snaps beans, cotton and Swiss chard were evaluated by the JMPR. These studies allowed deriving a general residue definition.
Animal: RD enf: Fen‐OH is not included in the residue definition for enforcement established at EU level. However, according to the results of the metabolism and livestock‐feeding studies, at the calculated dietary burden, residues in livestock are mainly driven by metabolite M03 (liver and kidney) and fenpyroximate (fat). Therefore, the difference in the residue definitions for enforcement in animal commodities can be considered as minor.
RD RA: Regarding the residue definition for risk assessment, metabolite M5 (free and its conjugates) is not included in the residue definition established in EU. It is noted that in the livestock‐feeding studies assessed by JMPR, M5 was not analysed in animal tissues and milk. According to the information available in the JMPR report, a conversion factor from enforcement to risk assessment was not derived to consider the exposure to this metabolite. Therefore, apparently the input values used by the JMPR for the risk assessment seem to consider only the levels of fenpyroximate, Fen‐OH and M‐3, which is in line with the EU residue definition. JMPR should be asked for clarifications as regards the metabolite M‐5 and its conjugates

Peer review: Prothioconazole‐desthio (sum of isomers)
Peer review and MRL review (in case DB increases): Sum of prothioconazole‐desthio and its glucuronide conjugate, expressed as prothioconazole‐desthio (not enforced).
The residue is fat soluble
efsa_comments:
The EU residue definition for risk assessment for plants is more comprehensive, covering all the metabolites containing the 2‐(1‐chlorocyclopropyl)‐3‐(2‐chlorophenyl)‐2‐hydroxypropyl‐2H‐1,2,4‐triazole moiety; conversion factors for enforcement to risk assessment were derived: 2 for cereal grain, pulses and oilseeds, leafy vegetables and root and tuber vegetables; 3 for cereal straw. Since for fruit crops metabolism, data are not available, a generic conversion factor for risk assessment is not available.
For animal commodities, the EU and JMPR risk assessment residue definitions are not identical. From the metabolism studies presented in the 2008 JMPR report, it seems that some of the major metabolites identified in animal commodities are not covered by the JMPR residue definition. The JMPR RA residue definition reflects those metabolites which were analysed in the cow‐feeding study.
The potential inclusion of glucuronide conjugate in the enforcement residue definition for all livestock matrices was recommended by the MRL review in case the EU livestock DB is increasing. From livestock metabolism studies, conversion factors from enforcement to risk assessment were derived as 2 for liver and 9 for kidney and 1 for other matrices.

JMPR: Fenazaquin
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Fenazaquin
Peer review: Fenazaquin (applicable to fruit);
efsa_comments:
The proposed enforcement RD for plants of JMPR is identical with the current EU residue definition established in the MRL legislation.
The other residue definitions are not fully compatible. The difference in residue definition for animal products is currently of no relevance as regards the proposed Codex MRLs (MRL proposals only for plant products).
For plants products, the peer review suggested two separate RA RDs (see above) based on a metabolism study in grapes.
Rationale (EFSA, 2013d): For fenazaquin and metabolite TBPE, separate risk assessments are conducted due to the different toxicological reference values (TBPE is of higher toxicity than fenazaquin).
JMPR assessed two metabolism studies in apples, one in oranges, grapes and maize. TBPE was not considered as a relevant metabolite by JMPR. It accounted for 2–5% of TRR in apples, < 6% of TRR in grapes (< 0.16 mg eq./kg): In oranges and maize, it was not identified. (This information should be verified in the JMPR evaluation).
As regards the separate RD RA for plants (TBPE), the RMS noted that no further in‐depth evaluation could be conducted on the continued need for setting of a 2nd RD for TBPE, and the EU position stands as it is. However, for benefits of aligning RD between JMPR and EU as much as possible it is strongly recommended to revisit this question as soon as possible, thereby taking into account potentially new data and new tools (QSAR) which were not available in the course of the peer review in order to decide whether such a high UF of 10 000 is further justified

JMPR: Sum of fosetyl, phosphonic acid and their salts, expressed as phosphonic acid
EU:
Sum of fosetyl, phosphonic acid and their salts expressed as phosphonic acid
MRL review: Phosphonic acid; risk managers to decide whether a separate residue definition for fosetyl should be established (EFSA, 2012h), confirmed by expert meeting (February 2018)
efsa_comments:
The residue definitions for enforcement in plant and animal commodities are expressed differently, i.e., as fosetyl or as phosphonic acid. The conversions between both compounds using conversion factors derived from molecular weights are possible.
For animal products, different residue definitions for enforcement are established. In the EU RD, fosetyl is included while JMPR restricted the RD to phosphonic acid. However, fosetyl is rapidly degrading to phosphonic acid in plants and in animals. Thus, the difference of the enforcement residue definitions for animal products is of low practical relevance. The RMS noted that in the RAR the same residue definition as the one set by JMPR was proposed.
The proposal to set the residue definitions for both risk assessment and monitoring as phosphonic acid only and to let risk managers decide to set a separate residue definition for fosetyl was discussed during the Standing Committee on the food chain and animal health held in Brussels on February 2014. Member States agreed to the proposal to set the residue definition as ‘phosphonic acid’. Nevertheless, pending modification of the existing enforcement residue definition (set in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005), the Article 10 MRL applications submitted to EFSA have been assessed in a way to accommodate various residue definitions.
The renewal of the approval of fosetyl‐Al at the European level is currently ongoing where the residue definitions for fosetyl‐Al in plant and animal matrices will be agreed.
When CXLs for plant and animal commodities are taken over in the EU MRL legislation, they need to be converted to fosetyl by applying the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.34.
Alternatively, if the EU residue definition is amended as proposed in the peer review, the CXLs can be taken over without recalculation, with a minor discrepancy for the MRLs for animal products

JMPR: Propamocarb
EU:
EU Reg. 2018/832:
Propamocarb (Sum of propamocarb and its salts, expressed as propamocarb)
efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: The residue definition set for enforcement and risk assessment by JMPR and at EU level are substantially the same
Animal commodities: The residue definition set for enforcement and risk assessment by JMPR and at EU level EU are quite different
EFSA proposed to limit the residue definition for enforcement to the best marker compound, identified as N‐oxide propamocarb in tissues of ruminants (and pigs) and in milks and as N‐desmethyl propamocarb in poultry tissues and eggs (details are reported below as background information)
For risk assessment, the EU residue definition is more comprehensive and includes the major plant and animal metabolites. Based on metabolism studies, tentative conversion factors for risk assessment were proposed during the MRL review (4.25 for milk; 2.2 for ruminant kidney, 1.7 for ruminant liver and muscle; 1 for ruminant fat; 1.3 for all poultry tissues and eggs)
Overall, the residue definitions for animal products derived at EU level and by JMPR are not compatible
Both assessments concluded residues in products of animal origin are not fat soluble
According to the MRL review, in ruminants, metabolite N‐oxide propamocarb was the predominant metabolite of the total residues found in kidney (41% TRR – 0.044 mg/kg), liver (49% TRR – 0.203 mg/kg), muscle (40.5% TRR – 0.008 mg/kg) and also in milk (21% TRR – 0.012 mg/kg). Oxazolidine‐2‐one propamocarb occurred in significant amounts in kidney, liver and milk (14–23% TRR; 0.014–0.09 mg/kg). 2‐hydroxy propamocarb was the major metabolite of the total residues in milk (37.5% TRR – 0.022 mg/kg) but was also identified at a lower level in liver (5% TRR) and kidney (13% TRR). Parent propamocarb accounted for 24.6% TRR in muscle (0.005 mg/kg), 23.5% TRR in kidney (0.025 mg/kg), 6.2% TRR in liver (0.026 mg/kg) and 6.0% TRR in milk (0.003 mg/kg)
In poultry, the predominant compound of the total residues was the N‐desmethyl propamocarb in eggs (45% TRR), liver (22% TRR), muscle (29% TRR) and to a minor extend in fat (6% TRR) while the parent compound occurred at a lower level in all matrices (2–12% TRR). Bis desmethyl propamocarb and N‐oxide propamocarb accounted for less than 10% TRR. It is noted that a significant fraction of the radioactive residues remained uncharacterised in liver and muscle (32% and 41% TRR, respectively)

Residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment in plant commodities are comparable. Animal:
RD enf: Fen‐OH is not included in the residue definition for enforcement established at EU level. However, according to the results of the metabolism and livestock‐feeding studies, at the calculated dietary burden, residues in livestock consist mainly of metabolite M‐3 (liver and kidney) and fenpyroximate (fat). JMPR: Tebuconazole
EU:
MRL review Art. 12 (EFSA, 2011k): Tebuconazole (provisional)
Peer review (EFSA, 2014a): 1) Sum of enantiomers contained in tebuconazole
2) Specific TDM residue definitions applicable to all active substances of the triazole chemical class (TA, TLA, TAA, 1,2,4‐T) (EFSA, 2018p)
efsa_comments:
For plant commodities, the JMPR residue definition for enforcement is identical with the EU residue definition. For risk assessment, in addition to the parent compound, residue definitions for the triazole derivative metabolites (TDMs) were established in the EU (EFSA, 2018p).
It is noted that for post‐harvest uses in fruits, no metabolism studies are available (neither in the EU nor at Codex level). In the EU MRL review a study on grapes with foliar application was considered sufficiently representative for post‐harvest uses in citrus because it was carried out with short PHIs and parent tebuconazole was the only compound identified.
For animal commodities, the residue definitions derived by JMPR and at EU level differ, but since Codex MRLs are proposed only for plant products, the discrepancy is not relevant for the current assessment.
Since the TDMs are relevant for risk assessment (and not for enforcement purposes) this should not have any impact on the MRLs derived for tebuconazole. In addition, TDMs are not expected to occur in citrus fruits following post‐harvest treatment.

JMPR: Tolclofos‐methyl
EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Tolclofos‐methyl
Peer review (EFSA, 2018b): Tolclofos‐methyl (potato (tuber vegetables) and lettuce (leafy crops)
MRL review Art. 12 (EFSA, 2014r): Tolclofos‐methyl
efsa_comments:
For plant products, the residue definition for monitoring according to the JMPR and EU evaluation for potato (tuber vegetables) and lettuce (leafy crops) are comparable.
The residue definitions for risk assessment differ. The EU peer review concluded that metabolism in the crop groups was different. For root and tuber (potato), the residue definition includes tolclofos‐methyl and metabolite DM‐TM‐CH2OH expressed as tolclofos‐methyl; the ratio between the parent and DM‐TM‐CH2OH was 1:4. For leafy crops (lettuce) and soil treatment, it includes tolclofos‐methyl and the metabolites TM‐CH2OH‐conjugate and metabolite ph‐CH3‐conjugate, and is preliminary pending on toxicological information on the metabolites and/or field trials (data gap) (EFSA, 2018b).
The JMPR evaluation RD RA includes also the metabolite DM‐TM, a processing degradate of tolclofos‐methyl which occurred in a high temperature hydrolytic study (24–87% AR), and detected in heated potatoes and lettuce.
For animal products, the JMPR and EU evaluation residue definition for monitoring and for risk assessment are comparable. However, the EU residue definitions for monitoring and for risk assessment are provisional.
Finalisation of the EU residue definitions in animals is pending on the recalculation of the dietary burden once the decision on the residue definition for risk assessment for feed items is taken (full information was not available on the magnitude of metabolite residue DM‐TM‐CH2OH in the feed item potato). An indicative dietary burden was calculated, based on tolclofos‐methyl residues measured in residue trial, using an adjustment factor to take into account the metabolites not analysed. The trigger value for feeding studies for ruminant, swine and poultry was exceeded. efsa_comments:
The existing enforcement residue definitions set by JMPR and in the EU for plant and animal commodities are expressed differently, i.e. as fosetyl or as phosphonic acid. Conversion factors can be used to make the MRL proposals derived by JMPR compatible with the EU residue definitions.
For animal products, different residue definitions for enforcement are established. In the EU RD, fosetyl is included while JMPR restricted the RD to phosphonic acid. However, fosetyl is rapidly degrading to phosphonic acid in plants and in animals. Thus, the difference of the enforcement residue definitions for animal products is of low practical relevance.
The residue definitions of enforcement and risk assessment in commodities of plant and animal origin proposed by the EU peer review are the same as the ones derived by the JMPR. However, these residue definitions have not been enforced yet. Therefore, when CXLs for plant and animal commodities are taken over in the EU MRL legislation, they need to be converted to fosetyl by applying the molecular weight conversion factor of 1.34. Alternatively, if the EU residue definition is amended as proposed in the peer review, the CXLs can be taken over without recalculation, with a minor discrepancy for the MRLs for animal products.
For the risk assessment, the residue definitions proposed by the peer review are applicable.

EU:
MRL review Art. 12 (EFSA, 2011n):
Metconazole (sum of isomers)
Peer review (EFSA, 2006c):
Metconazole (sum of isomers) (cereals and oilseed crops only)
Separate RDs for TDMs
efsa_comments:
JMPR assessed metabolism studies in fruits (banana and mandarins), oilseed (peas and rape seed) and cereals (wheat). Metconazole was the predominant residues (19–96% TRRs) in all crops except, wheat grain where it was not found. In addition, significant residues of hydroxylated metconazole metabolites and their conjugates were found in.
Triazole metabolites (TDMs) were also found in significant amounts in wheat grain, oilseed rape seed and pea seeds.
M11, M21 and M30 were identified in metabolism studies; in residue trials they were only found in cereals. In order to decide whether they need to be included in the RD, JMPR calculated the exposure and compared it with the TTC for Cramer Class III (see toxicological reference values). Individually the long‐term exposure was below the TTC of 1.5 μg/kg bw per day (i.e. 0.81 μg/kg bw per day).
Significant residues of unidentified hydroxylated metconazole metabolites and their conjugates were detected in mandarin fruit, pea seed and oilseed rape seed, ranging from 19% to 67% TRRs. Also for these compounds JMPR estimated the long‐term exposure and compared it to the TTC for Cramer class III compounds. Since no residue data from treated crops were available, JMPR calculated the estimated concentration, taking into account the ratio of parent metconazole to these metabolites observed in metabolism studies. The exposure for the group of hydroxylated metconazole metabolites was 0.75 μg/kg bw per day.
Based on overall results, JMPR proposed for plants, the enforcement and risk assessment residue definitions as metconazole (sum of isomers) only.
Currently, in the EU the residue definition for enforcement and the risk assessment (plant products) are similar with what JMPR proposed.
In the ongoing EU peer review process a new residue definition for risk assessment is under discussion, i.e. metconazole (sum of isomers) and its monohydroxylated derivatives (free and conjugates).
Triazole metabolites were also considered for the dietary exposure and consequently, it was proposed to be included separately in the RA RD: 1) triazole alanine (TA) and triazole lactic acid (TLA) as they share the same toxicity, 2) triazole acetic acid (TAA); 3) 1,2,4‐triazole (T).
For animal products, the enforcement residue definition proposed by the JMPR is similar with the one from EU (the existing and the agreed under the peer review process).
For risk assessment the proposed JMPR residue definition is wider covering also the two monohydroxylated compounds M01 and M12 of metconazole.
In the ongoing EU peer review process a new residue definition for risk assessment is under discussion, which is comparable with the JMPR RD.
In the EU also the separate TDM residue definitions are relevant for risk assessment (/animal and plant products), 1) triazole alanine (TA) and triazole lactic acid (TLA) as they share the same toxicity; 2) triazole acetic acid (TAA); 3) 1,2,4‐triazole (T).
As regards, the fat solubility JMPR consider the residue of metconazole as not fat soluble while in EU is considered as fat soluble.

efsa_comments:
JMPR assessed metabolism studies in fruits (grapes), roots (potatoes) and leafy (lettuce) following foliar treatment. Valifenalate was the major residues in all investigated crops accounting between 66 and 99% of TRRs. For plants, JMPR proposed the enforcement residue definition as valifenalate. For the risk assessment, valifenalate acid was also included in the RD.
In the EU, based on the same metabolism studies, the residue definition for enforcement and risk assessment was derived as valifenalate.
The RDs for enforcement (plant and animal products) derived by JMPR are comparable with the EU residue definitions implemented in Reg. 396/2005.
The RD for risk assessment (animal products) is also comparable. However, the residue definition for RA derived by JMPR for plants is wider than the EU RD. Hence the input values for RA are likely to be more conservative.

JMPR: Metalaxyl (sum of enantiomers)
EU: Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M (metalaxyl including other mixtures of constituent isomers including metalaxyl-M (sum of isomers))
efsa_comments:
JMPR meeting assessed seven metabolism studies for primary crops on grapes (2 studies), lettuce (2 studies) and potato (3 studies) conducted with metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M. In grapes and potato tubers, metalaxyl represented the major compound (64% of TRR and 57% of TRR, respectively) while M8 accounted 20% of TRR in grapes and 4 of TRR in potato tubers. In lettuce, M8 was the main compound accounting up to 61% of TRR, mainly conjugated form), while metalaxyl represented 19% of TRR.
Since M8 was not analysed in the residue trials, JMPR derived conversion factors to recalculate the results of metalaxyl to the residue definition for risk assessment (CF 11 for leafy crops and 1.3 for fruits and non-leafy vegetables) No conversion factor required for bulb, root and tuber crops and for crops where no residues are expected to be found. Rotational crops metabolism studies were conducted with metalaxyl and metalaxyl-M in several crops covering all crops group of leafy, roots and cereals.
Various metabolites were found, SYN546555 a breakdown compound of M8 was major in wheat hay (40% TRR), M1 (20% sugar beet root), M5 (up to 45% TRR in wheat hay), M8 in wheat stalk (33% TRR), mature lettuce (up 21% TRR), radish leaves (19% TRR) and wheat forage (40% TRR). Metalaxyl was found > 10% only in radish leaves at 120-day PBI. Except SYN546555, all the other metabolites found in rotational crops were found in primary crops. EU RA RD for plants was limited to metalaxyl (sum of enantiomers).
It is noted that the primary metabolism studies evaluated in EU were not all the same (additional studies on tobacco, tomatoes and wheat considered). In the ongoing assessment on the renewal of the approval (AIR peer review), it was decided to exclude M8 from the RD RA due to its low occurrence levels observed in GAP-compliant field trials on grapes and tomatoes.
In the AIR peer review of metalaxyl-M, only a DEREK analysis was available for M8, but as it is structurally very related to CGA 108906 and SYN546520, for which several studies were available, it was considered toxicologically covered.
The available livestock metabolism shows that metalaxyl is rapidly metabolised to various components free and conjugates with M3 being the major residue in milk and muscle (70% TRR in milk and 30% hen muscle), M6 (max 31% TRR tissues) M8 (max 34% TRR in kidney), M1 and M7 in goat muscle (max 14% TRR) and fat (40% of TRR). Metalaxyl was recovered only in eggs for 6% TRR. Although no metabolism studies with metalaxyl-M were available is not expected to lead to formation of different compounds.
Analytical methods for animal products were mainly based on common moiety methods; the methods were not sufficiently validated for the metabolites. JMPR did not propose CXL for animal commodities, because no validated analytical methods are available that include the determination of metabolites. In the EU assessment, the EU MRLs for animal products were tentatively set, requesting analytical methods for enforcement for animal products.
This data gap was not addressed in the framework of the confirmatory data assessment, and therefore, EFSA suggested further risk management considerations for animal products (EFSA, 2021i).

EU: Reg. 396/2005 (implementing MRL review): Prothioconazole-desthio (sum of isomers) Peer review (EFSA, 2007): Sum of prothioconazole-desthio and its glucuronide conjugate, expressed as prothioconazole-desthio The residue is fat soluble
efsa_comments:
In the framework of the renewal of the approval of prothioconazole, the Pesticides Peer Review Teleconference 25 (28–29 September 2020) confirmed the RD enforcement for plant and animal products (prothioconazole-desthio (M04) (sum of isomers)); New provisional RD for RA were proposed in this meeting for plants: Sum of prothioconazole-desthio (M04) and prothioconazole-desthio-3-hydroxy (M14), prothioconazole-desthio-4-hydroxy (M15), prothioconazole-desthio-5-hydroxy (M16), prothioconazole-desthio-6-hydroxy (M17) and prothioconazole-desthio-alpha-hydroxy (M18) and their conjugates expressed as prothioconazole-desthio.
The proposed RD are provision, pending submission of genotoxicity data on M15 and M17. (CF of 1 for root, tuber and pulses, and oilseed commodities and CF of 3 for cereal straw were proposed).
New provisional RD for RA for animal products: Sum of prothioconazole-desthio (M04) free and conjugated, prothioconazole-desthio-3-hydroxy (M14), prothioconazole-desthio-4-hydroxy (M15), prothioconazole-desthio-3,4-dihydroxy (M33), prothioconazole-desthio-4,5-dihydroxy (M35), free and their conjugates expressed as prothioconazole-desthio equiv.
The proposed RD is considered as provisional pending the submission of toxicity data to address the genotoxic potential and the general toxicity of M15, M33 and M35. (Proposed CF: 2 for liver, 4 for kidney based on the goat metabolism, no CF for milk, muscle and fat since the residue levels in these matrices are expected to be negligible). In addition, RD for TDMs were proposed for plant and animal products (RD RA):
  * • TA and TLA, since these compounds share the same toxicity,
  * • TAA,
  * • 1,2,4-triazole
JMPR did not establish residue definitions for risk assessment covering the TDMs. For prothioconazole, in principle, the conclusions from the EU pesticides peer review on the risk assessment for the triazole derivative metabolites (TDMs) in the light of confirmatory data would also apply on the need to consider TDMs in the residue definitions.
The EU residue definition for risk assessment for plants is more comprehensive, covering all the metabolites containing the 2-(1-chlorocyclopropyl)-3-(2-chlorophenyl)-2-hydroxypropyl-2H-1,2,4-triazole moiety; conversion factors for enforcement to risk assessment were derived: 2 for cereal grain, pulses and oilseeds, leafy vegetables and root and tuber vegetables; 3 for cereal straw. Since for fruit crops metabolism data are not available, a generic conversion factor for risk assessment is not available.
For animal commodities, the EU and JMPR risk assessment residue definitions are different. From the metabolism studies presented in the 2008 JMPR report, it seems that some of the major metabolites identified in animal commodities are not covered by the JMPR residue definition. The JMPR RA residue definition reflects only those metabolites which were analysed in the cow-feeding study.
The potential inclusion of glucuronide conjugate in the enforcement residue definition for all livestock matrices was recommended by the MRL review in case the EU livestock DB is increasing. From livestock metabolism studies, conversion factors from enforcement to risk assessment were derived as 2 for liver and 9 for kidney and 1 for other matrices. As the renewal process is still ongoing, further modifications of the residue definitions might be proposed in the EU.

efsa_comments:
Since clothianidin is also the main metabolite of the active substance thiamethoxam and considering that clothianidin and thiamethoxam have different toxicological reference values, at EU level the residue definitions for plant products and products from ruminants and pigs were derived as clothianidin and thiamethoxam separately.
Since also JMPR considers the residues of clothianidin from the use as an active substance and from the use of thiamethoxam, these residue definitions can be considered comparable with the definitions derived by the JMPR. No residue definition was derived for poultry products during the EU MRL review since poultry was not expected to be exposed to significant residues of clothianidin or thiamethoxam.
In the reasoned opinion on the MRL review, EFSA considered the residue definitions derived by JMPR consistent with the findings of the metabolism studies available (EFSA, 2014r). This conclusion is still considered valid.

JMPR: Pydiflumetofen
EU: Reg. 396/2005: No specific MRLs established (default MRL according to Art. 18(1)(b) Peer review proposal (EFSA, 2019g): Pydiflumetofen
efsa_comments:
As the EU approval process is still ongoing, a final decision on the residue definitions has not yet been taken. Currently, the default residue definitions (Art. 18(1)(b)) are applicable for enforcement. The residue definitions proposed in the EFSA conclusion are comparable with the Codex residue definitions except for animal products (risk assessment).
For animal products (all matrices), a provisional residue definition for risk assessment was proposed, which covers the parent compound and 2,4,6-TCP. However, for 2,4,6-TPC, additional toxicological data were requested. As reported by the RMS, additional data on 2,4,6-TPC were assessed in a revised DAR which may be sufficient to derive a definitive RD for RA for animal products.
The JMPR residue definition for animal products (risk assessment) for mammalian liver and kidney is wider than the proposed provisional EU RD. The EU residue definitions for primary crops were proposed to be applied also to rotational crops. Pydiflumetofen is a very persistent compound (DT50 = 8,540 days EU value), the accumulation of residue and consequently the uptake from the soil cannot be neglected (see also the general comment from the MRL assessment).

JMPR: Flutianil
EU: Reg. 396/2005: Flutianil Peer review (EFSA, 2014n): Flutianil (fruits and leafy crops only)
efsa_comments:
The same metabolism studies were assessed by JMPR and EU. In the four metabolism studies in fruits (grapes, apples, cucumbers) and leafy (lettuce) flutianil was the major compound among all studies. Metabolites including OC 56635 also occurred in relevant amounts (> 10% of TRRs) but mainly in the non-edible part of the crops.
JMPR RD for plants: For risk assessment JMPR proposed a wider residue definition including also OC 56635) in RA RD for plant, considering the result from the grape trials were OC 56635 found > 0.01 mg/kg and the information from the rotational metabolism studies where this metabolite was shown to be the major one (83% of TRR) which was found to be highly persistent. EU RD for plants: Flutianil only, with additional data required for rotational crops.
The RMS informed EFSA that studies on rotational crops have been provided in the framework of the recent MRL application (EFSA, 2021g); a review of the current residue definition as regards the possible inclusion of metabolite OC 56635 should be considered. JMPR RD for animal commodities: A goat metabolism studies over dosed study (10 ppm for 5 days) showed flutianil metabolised into numerous compounds from 10% up 82% of TRRs but not identified. No metabolism studies on poultry were available.
Since the max dietary burden from current use was 0.06 mg/kg and no metabolism data in animal was available for OC 56635, JMPR considered not possible to derive a RA RD for animals. EU RD for animal commodities: No metabolism studies were triggered by the previous EU assessment (peer review and import tolerance application), therefore no RA-RD for animal was proposed. For monitoring, JMPR and EU considered flutianil was the best marker in plant and animals.
For the commodities for which Codex MRL proposals were derived by JMPR in 2019, the difference of residue definitions for risk assessment of plants is of low relevance since these Codex MRLs under discussion refer to permanent crops only.

efsa_comments:
The current residue definitions for enforcement established in Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 are not directly comparable with the residue definition proposed by JMPR which comprises also the enol‐metabolite. In the framework of the MRL review, the enol‐metabolite was proposed to be included in the residue definition for enforcement, but recommendations of this assessment have not yet been legally implemented.
As regards the risk assessment residue definition (RD‐RA), for plants, JMPR proposed to include not only the enol‐metabolite but also 4‐hydroxymethyl‐Sp‐enol, free and conjugated; the latter was not proposed by the peer review. In the framework of the Article 12 MRL review, two RD‐RA were proposed: (1) primary crops, except leafy crops including spiromesifen‐enol (M01) and (2) for leafy and rotational crops, also including enol (M01), spiromesifen‐4‐hydroxymethyl (M02) and its conjugate M03. It was noted that the inclusion of metabolites M04 and M06 in the residue definition for rotational leafy crops may need to be reconsidered, based on the outcome of a rotational field trial on succeeding leafy (EFSA, 2019a).
Since the proposed Codex MRLs are for fruits and pulses and oilseeds only, for which the RD‐RA is the same in the EU and JMPR, the difference in the RD‐RA derived by JMPR and the EU (for leafy crops and rotational crops) will not have an impact on the assessment.
It is noted that for animal products, residue definitions at the EU level could not be proposed in the absence of appropriate metabolism studies. There are no Codex MRL proposals for livestock commodities.

EU:

Fruits crops:
Fenazaquin

Fenazaquin
Peer review (EFSA, 2013d): Fenazaquin (applicable to fruit crops)
efsa_comments:
The EU and JMPR enforcement residue definitions for plants are nearly identical, covering only parent fenazaquin. In the EU, for risk assessment, a second residue definition was established for metabolite TBPE. Overall, EU residue definitions for both enforcement and risk assessment for plants are restricted to fruit crops while JMPR derived a global enforcement residue definition. Furthermore, the risk assessment RD for plants derived by JMPR was not used for the risk assessment of pulses and leafy vegetables, as it was derived from metabolism studies in two crop groups (cereals and fruit). Hence requests for setting CXLs for pulses and mint were rejected.
For animals there is a slight difference in the residue definition for enforcement and RA, since EFSA is proposing fenazaquin only (for ruminants), while JMPR proposes a wider RD which includes also metabolites, i.e. tautomeric forms of 4‐hydroxyquinazoline (only for risk assessment) and 2‐hydroxy‐fenazaquin acid (for enforcement and risk assessment).
The RMS informed EFSA that during the renewal of the approval, the residue definitions for plant products (enforcement and risk assessment) are confirmed (still restricted to fruits). The previous tentative residue definition for leafy vegetables is no longer supported by the RMS.
The residue definitions for ruminants are also confirmed during the renewal, but the RMS highlighted that the representative uses do not include feed items and therefore they are not required.

As regards the risk assessment residue definition for the crop group relevant in the current assessment (i.e. pulses and oilseeds), the RDs for RA derived by JMPR and in the EU are different: the JMPR proposed the sum of triflumuron and M02, expressed as triflumuron and M07, assessed separately.
Comment on EU RD for risk assessment:
Considering the TRV derived for parent and metabolite, the following EU residue definition for risk assessment were considered in this assessment:
for chronic risk assessment: sum of triflumuron, M07 and M08, expressed as triflumuron;
for acute risk assessment: sum of M07 and M08, expressed as M07.
As the EU assessment does not clearly specify, whether the ARfD derived for M07 is also applicable to M08, a worst‐case assumption was taken to assume that M08 shares the same toxicological profile as M07.
For animal products the RD for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and EU are the same (parent only).

Ruminants:
1) Mefentrifluconazole
2) TDMs, with a separate assessment of TA and TLA TAA1,2,4‐Triazole
Poultry:
1) Mefentriconazole and metabolite M750F022 and fatty acid conjugates of M750F022, expressed as parent.
2) TDMs, with a separate assessment of TA and TLA TAA 1,2,4‐Triazole
efsa_comments:
Plant commodities: In the primary crop metabolism studies conducted in grape, soya bean and wheat, mefentrifluconazole was the predominant compound in most of matrices (60–92% TRR) in forage (wheat, soya bean), leaf/stalk (grapevine), straw/hull/chaff (wheat, soya bean), green pod (soya bean) and grape (grapevine). In wheat grain and soya bean seed, mefentrifluconazole was present at very low levels, while TDMs (triazole metabolites, mainly triazole alanine) represented the predominant residues.
In a rotational crop metabolism study in leafy vegetables, root and tuber vegetables and cereals, mefentrifluconazole and TDM were identified as major residues, similar to the primary crops.
The ratio of R‐ and S‐enantiomers of mefentrifluconazole residues in plants remained unchanged compared with the test substance.
The residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment derived by JMPR and at EU level are identical. However, in the EU, additional risk assessment residue definitions comprising the TDMs were set.
Animal commodities:
In goat matrices, parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐triazole were the predominant components of the residue. Significant change in the ratio of S:R enantiomers was revealed in most of goat matrices with proportion of the R‐enantiomer of 70–80% in cream, muscle, liver, kidney and fat. A similar shift was observed in liver and kidney of rats.
In poultry matrices, the metabolite M750F022 (and its fatty acid conjugates) is the predominant component of the residue, with parent mefentrifluconazole and 1,2,4‐T also present as significant components.
Based on this data JMPR proposed the RD for enforcement as mefentrifluconazole (free and conjugated);
At EU level, the residue definition for enforcement only comprises the parent compound (without the conjugates).
EFSA considers the RD for enforcement derived by JMPR not appropriate, because
The individual conjugates are not sufficiently defined; to develop and validate enforcement methods, the individual components need to be available as analytical standards to check if the method is capable to analyse for them (e.g. efficiency of hydrolytic step to convert the conjugate to the unconjugated form).
Currently, no analytical methods are available for enforcement,
The conjugates of the parent compound are of minor relevance;
The parent compound is therefore considered to be an appropriate marker substance.
For risk assessment the JMPR and the EU RD are not comparable, as JMPR also included the conjugates of the parent compound (see discussion of RD for enforcement) and M750F022 (and its conjugates) for all animal products. As the samples of animal products derived in the feeding studies were not analysed for the conjugates, JMPR derived correction factors from the metabolism studies.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Isoflucypram (default MRLs/RD according to Art. 18(1)(b))
Peer review (EFSA, 2022d): Isoflucypram (for all crop groups following foliar application)
efsa_comments:
At EU level, the same metabolism studies (primary crops, rotational crops and livestock) were assessed as by JMPR.
Overall, EFSA proposed parent isoflucypram as the residue definition for MRL enforcement for plant and animal products.
The risk assessment, residue definitions for animal products is provisional; the residue definition for risk assessment for plant products is limited to cereals only (EFSA, 2022d). The same residue definition as in primary crops was proposed provisionally also for rotational and processed commodities.
JMPR proposed only a residue definition for enforcement as isoflucypram for plant and animal products. For risk assessment, JMPR could not derive a conclusion on the residue definition due to the lack of genotoxicity studies for two metabolites found in rotational crop studies exceeding 0.01 mg eq./kg in mature Swiss chard (i.e. M52 and M54). The dietary exposure for these two metabolites was above the TTC for compound with potential genotoxicity.
Details on metabolism studies:
Primary crops: Metabolism studies in tomatoes, wheat, soya bean and rapeseed following foliar application and on root potatoes following the postharvest treatment. Isoflucypram was the major compound in all edible parts of the crops (max 93% TRR in wheat grain, 98% TRR in tomato fruits, etc) and in cereals feed items (up to 63% TRR in straw and 55% TRR in hay). Other relevant compounds found in relative and/or absolute amount were: M01 (isoflucypram‐propanol) and M06 (isoflucypram desmethyl propanol) free and conjugates in wheat straw and hay, in soya bean forage and hay were found also the M44 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐homo GSM), M45 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐Cys‐MA), M46 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐OH), M47 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid‐Glyc), M48 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐mercapto‐lactic acid – propil‐OH‐Glyc) and M58 (isoflucypram‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide) in potato tuber.
M01 and M06 free and conjugates were found in residue trials on cereals (i.e grains) at levels either comparable or higher than the parent.
Based on metabolism studies and field trials the residue definition for risk assessment at EU level was proposed as: sum of isoflucypram, M01 and its conjugates, M06 and conjugates expressed as isoflucypram limited to cereals only. For enforcement the residue definition was proposed as isoflucypram.
JMPR considered M01 could be excluded from the risk assessment based on the results from residue trials, due to the low occurrence of quantifiable residues in cereals; M06 was assess by using the TTC approach (Cramer Class III) and was found not relevant for risk assessment by JMPR.
In rotational crops, several compounds such as M49 (BCS‐CR60082), M52 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐Cys) and M54 (isoflucypram‐desfluoro‐N‐methyl‐cyclopropyl‐pyrazole‐carboxamide‐OH‐GSH) occurred above 10% of TRRs, different than in primary crops. Isoflucypram was found only in wheat forage. For the metabolites M52 and M54, a potential concern for genotoxicity was identified at EU level. JMPR applied the TTC approach to assess M52 and M54, and concluded that the exposure was above the threshold for genotoxic compounds (0.0025 μg/kg bw per day).
Processing studies: Under standard hydrolysis conditions of pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation submitted during peer review isoflucypram and M01 are stable (98%). M06 degraded into M77 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol‐aldehyde) under boiling/brewing/baking up to 66% and under sterilisation up to 98%). Since for M77 a genotoxicity potential could not be excluded, in the EU peer review process, a data gap was set to address genotoxicity, since the precursor substance M06 was found in barley grain at relevant levels.
Animal metabolism studies: Isoflucypram was found in all animal tissues, in milk and eggs, liver and ruminant fat. M01 and M06 were recovered at relevant amount in almost all matrices, except M01 in milk and ruminant fat. M07 (isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐1,2 propandiol), M11 ((isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐carboxylic acid) and M12 isoflucypram‐carboxylic acid) were found above 10% TRRs in poultry muscle and liver. However, based on poultry feeding studies M07, these metabolites were not expected above 0.01 mg/kg. In ruminants, additional compound such as M02 (isoflucypram‐2 propanol), M19 (conjugate of M01), M20 (conjugate of M02) and M50 were found as relevant; in the EU assessment, for M50 (isoflucypram‐N‐methyl‐pyrazole carboxylic acid) the genotoxicity potential was considered not addressed.
JMPR identified the following information missing that would be desirable to derive proposals for residue definitions for plant and animal products:
Submission of cereal grain processing data for isoflucypram‐desmethyl‐propanol (M06)
Hydrolysis of the extracts from soya bean metabolism studies
In the EU assessment, potential concerns for genotoxicity based on positive genotoxicity QSAR predictions were identified (M50, M66, M67, M77).

EU:

efsa_comments:
At EU level, metabolism studies were available for fruits and mushrooms; JMPR had studies available for maize, soybean, apple, cabbage, cotton, orange, mushrooms, rice, wheat and beans, which were assessed in its previous assessments (JMPR 2002, 2011). For the current assessment, no new metabolism studies were reported
It would be desirable that JMPR in its assessment discusses the relevance of the metabolism studies and the appropriateness of the current residue definitions for the new uses assessed
For the commodity under discussion in this CCPR meeting (i.e. tea), the EU and Codex enforcement and risk assessment residue definitions are identical. However, in the EU, an additional residue definition was established, encompassing 4‐chloroaniline (PCA) a genotoxic carcinogen metabolite (EFSA). At EU level no metabolism studies are available for leafy crops to cover the Codex MRL proposal for tea
In the EU, standard hydrolysis studies with radiolabelled diflubenzuron were available to investigate the degradation of residues under conditions simulating pasteurisation, boiling/brewing/baking and sterilisation. Significant degradation of diflubenzuron occurred under sterilisation conditions (pH of 6, temperature 120°C), leading to the formation of PCA up to 58% of the applied radioactivity (AR), and the detection of 4‐chlorophenylurea (CPU) at 6%, a precursor of PCA
Tea is primarily consumed as an infusion prepared from fermented/dried tea leaves with boiling water. Information on the formation of PCA during fermentation/drying is not available. The pH of tea infusions is neutral/slightly acidic; for green tea infusions. In standard hydrolysis studies, the formation of PCA was not observed under boiling conditions (pH 5, 100°C), EFSA is of the opinion that the available data do not allow to exclude the presence of PCA in tea infusion (100°C, neutral or slightly acidic pH)
The transfer of diflubenzuron residues from tea leaves into tea infusions was assessed by JMPR. In this study, the possible formation of PCA was not investigated

EU:
Reg. 396/2005:
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
MRL review (EFSA, 2017c):
Root crops:
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
Processed potato (tentative):
1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
efsa_comments:
Plants (root)
: Metabolism studies in potatoes are available, where 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene was the major component identified in the whole tuber (79–93% TRRs), in peeled potato and potato peel (57–94% TRR). Additionally, in peeled potato, metabolite M21 accounted for up to 20% TRR 30 days after the sixth application, while M23 was either not detected or in low proportions. Other minor polar compounds were detected after six applications (7–10% TRR) further identified as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthol and glycoside conjugates of metabolite M21. Based on these results, the residue for enforcement was defined as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene while for risk assessment it was defined as sum of 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and M21 and its conjugates expressed as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
At JMPR level the same metabolism study was assessed. JMPR derived an enforcement residue definition similar to the EU, while for risk assessment a slightly different residue definition was proposed, which does not comprise the glucoside conjugates of M21. However, their contribution to the dietary exposure is expected to be insignificant
Processed commodities:
Standard hydrolysis studies to investigate 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene, M21 and M23 were not available at the EU level. However, a study simulating household processing of potatoes (boiling, frying and baking) was conducted with radiolabelled 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and submitted under the MRL review (EFSA, 2021c)
In all samples of processed potatoes, 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene was the major compound identified (47–58% TRR), while M21 and M23 were identified at 0.5%–7.2% TRR and < 0.6%–5.6% TRR, respectively. In the MRL application (EFSA, 2023g), additional confirmation was provided for the compounds provisionally identified as glycoside conjugates of M21 and 1,4‐dimethylnaphthol during the MRL review. The same residue definitions as for plants are applicable for processed commodities
Based on the same processing study in potatoes, JMPR concluded that for dietary intake of processed commodities, the same residue definition as for unprocessed products should apply
Animal commodities:
Livestock metabolism studies were conducted with 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene. In goat study the major compound found was the conjugate of M23, accounting for 18% and 16% TRR in milk and in kidney, respectively, while the parent was rapidly absorbed and excreted. In poultry M23 (free and conjugated) was the major compound accounting up to 71% of TRRs in all matrices except fat, where the parent compound was the most predominant (94% of TRRs). 1,4‐Dimethylnaphthalene was also present in eggs and muscle at relevant amounts (29–35% TRR). The residue definitions at EU level for both, enforcement and risk assessment were defined as the sum of 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene and its metabolite M23 (free and conjugated), expressed as 1,4‐dimethylnaphthalene
JMPR derived a slightly different residue definition for animal matrices except milk based on the same livestock metabolism studies, including the glycine conjugate of M23, while in the EU residue definition, free and conjugated M23 was included, without specifying the type of conjugate. For milk, JMPR proposed a separate residue definition
The EURLs noted that 1,4‐DMN and other DMN‐isomers may occur naturally in various plants (EFSA, 2021c). DMN isomers also occur in mineral oils (naphtha), that are commonly used in agriculture, either as adjuvants in plant protection products or even as active ingredients

efsa_comments:

The residue definition for risk assessment for plants in the EU is maleic hydrazide (restricted to foliar treatment on root crops only).
The latest peer‐review (EFSA, 2025i) considered the additional toxicological data available on 3‐pyridazinone leading to a separate ADI for this metabolite (see Section 1.1.2). Therefore, the expression of the risk assessment residue definition in animal commodities was proposed.

For paddy rice:
No conclusion on the suitability of the RD for other plant commodities

Peer review (EFSA, 2010c,  2025c):
Provisional, pending confirmation by a review to current standards): Sum of buprofezin and BF4 conjugates analysed as BF9 + BF12 under acidic conditions and expressed as buprofezin.
(N.B. In the renewal process, only non‐edible crops were assessed. No RD for RA were established.)
efsa_comments:
EU: For plant and animal products, the default RD for MRL enforcement is applicable (i.e. parent compound only), as no EU uses/import tolerances for food commodities.
Metabolism studies in livestock were not evaluated in the recent peer review (EFSA, 2025c). In case an animal residue definition would become necessary, a re‐evaluation of the livestock metabolism studies and toxicological data on the pertinent metabolites to current standards would be required. For plant commodities, the residue definition derived in 2010 was proposed on provisional basis. In the framework of the renewal process (EFSA, 2025c), which was restricted to non‐food and non‐feed crops, data on metabolites of buprofezin that could be important for the consumer dietary risk assessment were not provided. Therefore, the residue definition for risk assessment was not established and no consumer risk assessment was finalised.
JMPR: The parent compound was considered a sufficient marker for MRL enforcement; for paddy rice, appropriate metabolism studies were not available to conclude on the appropriate residue definition (as paddy rice may take up metabolites from sediment/water systems, JMPR concluded that radio‐labelled metabolism studies on paddy rice and radio‐labelled degradation studies in water/sediment systems are needed to assess the appropriateness of the current residue definitions). The RD for RA for other plant products (except paddy rice) and for animal products is restricted to buprofezin.

EU:
Reg. 396/2005: Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl
Peer review (EFSA, 2018b): Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl (cereals only)
efsa_comments:
Plants:
At JMPR level
, four crops were investigated in primary metabolism studies: cereals (wheat (foliar) and rice (various applications)), fruits (soil) and pulses and oilseed (foliar), using labels at [PY‐], [PH‐] and [BE‐] positions. For rice, foliar flooded, water injected and dry‐seeded scenarios were investigated.
Florpyrauxifen‐benzyl was extensively metabolised across all investigated crops, with X11966341 and X11438848 identified as the major metabolites in both free and conjugated forms. These metabolites were primarily observed in plant parts used as feed items, forage with X11966341 up to 47% TRR and X11438848 up to 17% TRR. In contrast, residues in seeds and wheat grains were minor (< 0.004 mg eq/kg).
In rice grain, residues exceeded 0.01 mg eq/kg in only one scenario, showing the same metabolic pattern as other plant parts: florpyrauxifen‐benzyl (max. 6% of TRRs), X11966341 and X11438848 each < 4% of TRRs. In apple metabolism studies, no transfer of residues to the plant was observed following soil treatment.
In the EU, similar metabolism studies on rice were available during peer review. Based on those studies, the residue definitions for enforcement and risk assessment were derived for cereals only. In the expression of the RA‐RD, it was provisionally assumed that X11966341 is covered by the parent toxicity. JMPR has not considered necessary a RA‐RD, while for enforcement, similar residue definition for all plant commodities was derived. However, EFSA is of the opinion that additional metabolism studies in fruits via foliar application would be needed to confirm whether the metabolic pattern is similar. Currently, no CXLs for fruits are evaluated.
Animal: Similar metabolism studies were assessed at both JMPR and EU levels in poultry and goat. Most of the radioactivity was excreted (97% of TRRs), with only minimal amount found in animal tissues. In poultry, residues were less than 0.01 mg eq/kg. In ruminants, X11966341 (up to 25% TRRs) and X11438848 (up to 45% TRRs) were recovered only in kidney and liver, while the parent compound was never detected. In other tissues, residues were < 0.01 mg eq/kg, and no further identification was performed.
Based on these findings, the residue definition for enforcement was derived in the EU as florpyrauxifen‐benzyl by default, while at the JMPR level, two metabolites were included. For risk assessment, JMPR did not consider it necessary to propose a residue definition. It is highlighted that the use assessed under EU peer review did not trigger the livestock assessment.
